entities.name: Industrial Age
entities.label: Timeframe
entities.summary:
The Industrial Age, spanning approximately 1760 CE to 1840 CE, marks a watershed period in human history, fundamentally transforming global economies, societies, and technologies. As a distinct sub-period of the broader Modern era, it witnessed an unprecedented shift from agrarian and handicraft economies to industrial and machine-based manufacturing. This era is defined by the mechanization of production, the emergence of the factory system, and the harnessing of new energy sources, laying the groundwork for the modern world system.

Key achievements include James Watt's significant improvements to the steam engine in the 1760s, revolutionizing power generation for factories and transportation. Innovations in textile production, such as Richard Arkwright's water frame (1769) and Edmund Cartwright's power loom (1785), propelled Britain to become the "workshop of the world." The development of new iron production methods, notably by Abraham Darby III at Coalbrookdale, enabled the construction of robust machinery and infrastructure, while the rise of the railway system in the early 19th century dramatically accelerated trade and communication.
